meta.title: Who really said "I attribute my success to this: I never gave or took any excuse"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Florence Nightingale genuinely wrote this in an 1861 letter (printed by Cook, 1913). But her words were 'an excuse' — the popular 'any excuse' is a later one-word drift.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I attribute my success to this: I never gave or took any excuse'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, it's really Florence Nightingale — from an 1861 letter. But she wrote 'an excuse'; 'any excuse' is a later corruption. The documented source and story.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This one is genuine. Nightingale wrote it in an 1861 private letter to Miss H. Bonham Carter, first printed in Sir Edward Cook’s The Life of Florence Nightingale (1913), vol. 1, p. 506. Her exact words, though, were “I never gave or took an excuse” — the widely shared “any excuse” is a later one-word drift, first documented around 2002 per Quote Investigator.

source.heading: The documented source
source.excerpt: I have had a larger responsibility of human lives than ever man or woman had before. And I attribute my success to this:—I never gave or took an excuse. Yes, I do see the difference now between me and other men. When a disaster happens, I act and they make excuses.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the earliest instance to Nightingale’s 1861 letter, printed in Sir Edward Cook’s The Life of Florence Nightingale (1913), vol. 1, p. 506 — wording “an excuse.”
Wikiquote’s sourced section likewise cites the 1861 letter to Miss H. Bonham Carter and gives the wording as “an excuse.”
Per QI’s timeline, faithful reprints (Eton College Chronicle 1914; Bradford 1933) kept “an excuse”; the swapped “any excuse” surfaces only around 2002.
source.excerptNote: From the 1861 letter as printed in Cook’s biography. The only context for the “disaster” is Nightingale’s own line in the same passage — “When a disaster happens, I act and they make excuses” — and Quote Investigator traces the line’s textual chronology without recording any further detail about the incident behind it.
source.rightsNote: The line comes from an 1861 letter and was first published in Sir Edward Cook’s biography in 1913. Both the letter and that first printing predate 1931, so the text is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Florence Nightingale
author.heading: About Florence Nightingale
author.metaLine: 1820–1910 · English social reformer, statistician & founder of modern nursing
author.bio: Florence Nightingale (1820–1910) rose to fame organising nursing care for British soldiers during the Crimean War, where her insistence on sanitation and record-keeping cut death rates dramatically. A pioneering statistician as well as a reformer, she founded the first scientifically based nursing school and reshaped hospital administration. The line about excuses comes from her private correspondence and reflects the relentless, accountability-driven temperament that defined her work.

misattribution.heading: The wording, not the author, is the problem
misattribution.intro: Unusually for a “famous name” quote, the attribution here is correct — Florence Nightingale really did write it. What’s been altered is a single word.

items.why: Nightingale’s 1861 letter, as printed in Cook’s 1913 biography, reads “I never gave or took an excuse.” Faithful early reprints kept “an”; the swap to “any” is first documented around 2002, per Quote Investigator.

misattribution.truthLine: Right author, near-right words: Nightingale wrote “an excuse” in an 1861 letter (Wikiquote, sourced); “any excuse” is a later one-word corruption.

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: Nightingale wrote the line in 1861, a few years after the Crimean War had made her a national figure. In the same passage she draws the contrast that gives the sentiment its bite: “When a disaster happens, I act and they make excuses.”

The quote spread widely only after Cook’s 1913 biography put the letter into print, and it has since become a staple of nursing and leadership motivation — usually in its slightly worn-down “any excuse” form.
